title: Acids, bases and salts
summary: Learn the definitions of acids and bases, pH, Ka, neutralization, salts and titration.
cards.0.p: Acids taste sour. Solutions of bases taste bitter and feel slippery. Dyes that change color in acids and bases are called indicators. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.
cards.0.svg#21: An indicator changes color over a certain pH range.
cards.0.key: Lemons and vinegar contain acids. Acids release CO₂ from limestone (CaCO₃), and this is how descalers work. Never taste anything in the lab.
cards.0.once.soru: You dip litmus paper into lemon juice. What color does it turn?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Lemon contains acid, and litmus turns red in acid.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Litmus turns blue in base. Lemon is acidic.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Litmus is an indicator, and its color changes in acid.
cards.1.p: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that releases H+ in water. The H+ bonds to water and forms H₃O+. A base is a substance that releases OH− in water. NH₃ is a base because it forms OH− with water.
cards.1.svg#6: The definition applies only to aqueous solutions.
cards.1.etk.soru: Sort each substance by how it behaves in water: does it release H⁺ or form OH⁻?
cards.1.etk.ogeler.3.2: This is acetic acid, found in vinegar. It releases H⁺ in water (weak acid).
cards.1.etk.ogeler.7.2: It has no OH in its structure, but it reacts with water and forms OH⁻.
cards.1.key: H₃O⁺ is the hydronium ion. The Arrhenius definition holds only for aqueous solutions.
cards.1.once.soru: Which ion does HCl release when it dissolves in water?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: HCl splits into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water. A substance that releases H⁺ in water is an acid.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: HCl has no OH group. Substances that release OH⁻ are bases.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: HCl splits almost completely into ions in water.
cards.2.p: According to Brønsted–Lowry, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. An acid that gives away a proton leaves behind its conjugate base. For example, the conjugate base of CH₃COOH is CH₃COO−.
cards.2.svg#15: HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s): no water, still acid–base
cards.2.key: An acid and its conjugate base differ by one H⁺. Water can both donate and accept a proton, so it is amphiprotic. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
cards.2.once.soru: What does water do in the reaction NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Water gives an H⁺ to NH₃ and becomes OH⁻. Here it acts like an acid.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: NH₃ is the one that accepts the proton and becomes NH₄⁺.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water reacts, loses an H⁺ and becomes OH⁻.
cards.3.p: Pure water ionizes slightly and reaches equilibrium (2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻). At 25 °C, Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴. In pure water both ions have a concentration of 10⁻⁷ M.
cards.3.svg#12: At 25 °C the product is always 1×10⁻¹⁴ M²
cards.3.key: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate. Kw increases with temperature. That is why neutral water does not have a pH of exactly 7 at temperatures other than 25 °C.
cards.3.once.soru: A little acid is added to pure water. What happens to [OH⁻]?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: At 25 °C the product [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] is constant. So when H₃O⁺ goes up, OH⁻ goes down.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The acid adds H₃O⁺. The product stays constant, so OH⁻ cannot increase.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: The product is constant. When one goes up, the other has to go down.
cards.4.h: pH, pOH and the pH scale
cards.4.p: pH is calculated as pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. For example, if [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, then pH = 3. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.
cards.4.key: pOH is calculated as pOH = −log[OH⁻]. If the pH drops by one unit, [H₃O⁺] goes up 10 times. If it drops by 2 units, it goes up 100 times.
cards.4.etk.soru: At 25 °C, [H₃O⁺] = a × 10<sup>−b</sup> M. Change the concentration: how do pH and pOH change?
cards.5.h: Strong and weak acids and bases
cards.5.p: Strong acids and bases such as HCl, HNO₃, NaOH and KOH ionize completely in water. Weak ones such as CH₃COOH in vinegar and NH₃ ionize only slightly. Being strong does not mean being concentrated.
cards.5.key: H₂SO₄ gives up its first proton completely. At the same concentration a strong acid has a lower pH. Dilute HCl is still a strong acid.
cards.6.p: The ionization of a weak acid is an equilibrium, written as Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Water is left out of this expression. The larger Ka is, the stronger the acid. Kb is written the same way for bases.
cards.6.key: If Ka is large, the acid is strong and the Kb of its conjugate base is small.
cards.6.once.soru: Ka values: 7×10⁻⁴ for HF and 1.8×10⁻⁵ for CH₃COOH. Which is the stronger acid?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The acid with the larger Ka ionizes more. HF has the larger Ka.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: This acid has the smaller Ka and ionizes less.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The Ka values differ. The one with the larger Ka is stronger.
cards.7.p: For a strong monoprotic acid, [H₃O⁺] equals the acid concentration. For example, 0.01 M HCl has a pH of 2. For weak acids, use [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C).
cards.7.key: For strong bases, find pOH first. If you dilute a strong acid 10 times, the pH goes up by 1. 0.01 M HCl has a pH of 2, and 0.001 M HCl has a pH of 3.
cards.7.once.soru: What is the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: HCl ionizes completely. [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is the concentration. pH is the negative logarithm of the concentration.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: 11 is the pOH. The pH of an acid is below 7.
cards.8.p: When an acid reacts with a base, a salt and water form. The real event is H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ joining to make water, and heat is released. Stomach remedies called antacids work this way.
cards.8.key: Antacids contain Mg(OH)₂ or NaHCO₃. Neutralization does not always give pH 7. The result depends on the salt that forms.
cards.9.p: H₂SO₄ can release two H⁺ and H₃PO₄ three. Ca(OH)₂ also releases two OH⁻. For complete neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻).
cards.9.svg#18: CH₃COOH has 4 H but releases only 1 H⁺.
cards.9.key: For example, 100 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ releases 0.02 mol of H⁺. 100 mL of 0.2 M NaOH neutralizes it. CH₃COOH releases only one H⁺.
cards.9.once.soru: How many moles of NaOH are needed to fully neutralize 0.1 mol of H₂SO₄?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺. 0.2 mol of H⁺ needs 0.2 mol of OH⁻.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Each H₂SO₄ releases two H⁺, but each NaOH releases only one OH⁻.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The acid is diprotic. So you need more base, not less.
cards.10.p: The anion of a weak acid or the cation of a weak base reaches equilibrium with water, and this is called hydrolysis. So the pH of a salt depends on the strength of the acid and base that formed it.
cards.10.key: The salt takes on the character of whichever side is strong. NH₄Cl is acidic and CH₃COONa is basic. If both are weak, compare Ka and Kb.
cards.11.p: Neutralizing an acid of unknown concentration drop by drop with a base of known concentration is called titration. When the acid is used up exactly, the equivalence point is reached and the pH jumps sharply.
cards.11.svg#10: 25 mL 0.1 M CH₃COOH also needs 25 mL
cards.11.key: For a weak acid, the total amount of acid still counts. In a strong acid–strong base titration, the pH at the equivalence point is 7. In a weak acid–strong base titration, it is above 7.
cards.11.once.soru: How many mL of NaOH of the same concentration are needed to neutralize 25 mL of HCl?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: If the concentrations are equal, equal volumes contain equal moles. So 25 mL is enough.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: That adds twice as much base. The acid runs out halfway, and the rest of the base is left over.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: That is half of what is needed. Half of the acid stays un-neutralized.
cards.12.p: A solution that contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa) is a buffer. When a little acid or base is added, its pH changes very little.
cards.12.svg#0: Adding 0.01 mol HCl to 1 L of solution
cards.12.key: A weak base with its conjugate acid also makes a buffer. Blood is protected by the H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ buffer. A buffer's capacity is limited.
cards.13.p: Active metals react with acids to form a salt and H₂. Cu, Ag and Au do not give H₂ with HCl. Amphoteric metals such as Al and Zn also release H₂ with strong bases.
cards.13.key: When diluting, always add acid to water, never water to acid. Cu and Ag react with HNO₃, but they release NO or NO₂, not H₂.
cards.14.p: Most nonmetal oxides are acidic (CO₂, SO₂). Oxides of active metals are basic (Na₂O, CaO). Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric, and CO, NO and N₂O are neutral oxides.
cards.14.svg#3: gives a salt with a base
cards.14.svg#7: gives a salt with an acid
cards.14.key: An acidic oxide forms an acid with water, and a basic oxide forms a base. In acid rain, SO₂ and NO₂ in the air form acids in rainwater.
cards.14.once.soru: What is the solution like when CO₂ dissolves in water?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: CO₂ forms carbonic acid with water. That is where the slight sourness of soda comes from.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Basic solutions come from metal oxides. C is a nonmetal.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: CO₂ reacts with water and forms an acid.
cards.15.p:
• An acid donates a proton and a base accepts one.
• At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, and pH 7 is neutral.
• Strong acids and bases ionize completely, weak ones only partly.
• In neutralization, n(H⁺) = n(OH⁻). The salt that forms is not always neutral.
• Active metals form a salt and H₂ with acids.
quiz.0.q: What is the pH of a 0.005 M Ca(OH)₂ solution at 25 °C? (Ca(OH)₂ ionizes completely.)
quiz.0.e: Each Ca(OH)₂ releases two OH<sup>−</sup>. So [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 M and pOH = 2. The pH is 14 − 2 = 12.
quiz.1.q: At 25 °C, a 0.01 M solution of the weak acid HA has K<sub>a</sub> = 1×10⁻⁶. What is the pH of the solution?
quiz.1.e: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K<sub>a</sub>·C) = √(10⁻⁶ × 10⁻²) = √(10⁻⁸) = 10⁻⁴ M, so pH = 4. HCl at the same concentration would have a pH of 2.
quiz.2.q: Match each oxide to its type.
quiz.2.e: CO₂ forms an acid with water, and CaO forms a base. ZnO reacts with both acids and bases. CO reacts with neither, so it is neutral.
quiz.3.q: A 0.1 M CH₃COOH solution is titrated with 0.1 M NaOH. Which is true for the solution at the equivalence point at 25 °C?
quiz.3.e: At equivalence the solution contains CH₃COONa. The anion of the weak acid reacts with water and releases OH<sup>−</sup>, so the solution is basic.
quiz.3.y.0: Equal moles of a weak acid and a strong base do not give a neutral solution. CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> reacts with water and produces OH<sup>−</sup>.
quiz.3.y.1: At the equivalence point all of the acid has reacted. The CH₃COO<sup>−</sup> left in solution makes it basic.
quiz.3.y.2: The pH reaches 14 only with 1 M OH<sup>−</sup>. Here there is only acetate, a weak base.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Explore the pH scale, neutralize an acid with a base and test a buffer.
A:adimlar.0.metin: pH 7 is neutral. Move along the scale and find a substance that turns litmus blue.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: Substances with a pH above 7 are basic and turn litmus blue. Soap, ammonia and bleach are examples.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The container holds 1 L of pure water at pH 7. Add 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH with the droppers. The pH meter, the color and the ions change instantly. Find the following yourself.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Add acid to bring the pH to 3.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: 1 mL of 1 M HCl in 1 L of water makes [H₃O⁺] 1×10⁻³ M, so pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. [OH⁻] dropped to 1×10⁻¹¹ M, and the product is still 1×10⁻¹⁴.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Now lower the pH to 2. How much acid did it take?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: To lower the pH by just 1 unit, you made the acid 10 times larger (from 1 mL to 10 mL). The pH scale is logarithmic, so each unit means a 10× difference in [H₃O⁺].
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Add NaOH to make the container basic: pH 11.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The OH⁻ ions first joined the H₃O⁺ ions to form water. The excess made the pH 11 (pOH = 3, pH + pOH = 14). Near the equal amount, a single drop makes the pH jump by several units.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Compare HCl and vinegar acid at the same concentration (0.1 M). Look at the ions and the lamp.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What makes vinegar acid a weak acid?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Strong and concentrated are not the same thing. Both are 0.1 M, and dilute HCl is still a strong acid.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: CH₃COOH has 4 H, but only one can be given away as a proton. Strength is about the fraction of protons given away.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Only about 1 percent of 0.1 M vinegar acid ionizes. The solution has little H₃O⁺, its pH is about 2.9 and the lamp is dim. HCl ionizes completely and has a pH of 1.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Add 0.1 M NaOH from the burette to fully neutralize 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl. The moles of acid and base must be equal. The flask contains phenolphthalein.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: The moles of acid and base must be equal. 25 mL × 0.1 M = 2.5 mmol.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: 2.5 mmol of NaOH fully neutralized 2.5 mmol of HCl. NaCl and water formed and the pH became 7. Right after the equivalence point the pH jumps sharply and phenolphthalein turns pink. This method is called titration.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Now you fully neutralized a weak acid, vinegar acid, with NaOH. The container holds sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) and water.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What is the pH of this salt solution?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The acid is all used up. Does the acetate ion left behind donate a proton or accept one?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That would be true for a strong acid and a strong base.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻) is the conjugate base of a weak acid, and it takes a proton from water (CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻). Because of the OH⁻ that forms, the pH is about 8.7.
A:adimlar.5.metin: One of the containers holds a mixture of vinegar acid and sodium acetate, that is, a buffer. Add the same amount of HCl to both containers and watch how their pH changes.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Why does the buffer's pH change so little?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The reaction CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O takes place. The added acid turns into a weak acid, so the pH drops very little.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Both containers have the same volume (100 mL). The difference is in the reaction, not in dilution.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The buffer is already acidic (pH 4.74) and contains H₃O⁺. What matters is what the added acid turns into.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Active metals react with acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂). You will put magnesium, zinc and copper into three tubes.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: In which tube do no H₂ bubbles form?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Magnesium is very active and bubbles the fastest.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Copper is less active than hydrogen and gives no H₂ with HCl. Silver and gold don't either.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Zinc also gives H₂ with acid, but more slowly than magnesium.
A:kapanis.0: pH 7 is neutral, below it is acidic and above it is basic. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.
A:kapanis.1: pH is logarithmic, and a drop of one unit makes [H₃O⁺] 10 times larger. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.
A:kapanis.2: Strong acids ionize completely, weak acids only partly. Strong and concentrated are not the same thing.
A:kapanis.3: An acid and a base form a salt and water. A salt solution is not always neutral. A buffer keeps pH changes small.
A:kapanis.4: Active metals form a salt and H₂ with acids. Cu, Ag and Au give no H₂ with HCl.
